newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says will not accept conditions from EU.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says will not accept conditions from EU.

text.p: The government, asked about a Spanish proposal for the European Union to take a stance urging democratic reforms in Cuba, said on Thursday it would not accept conditions for relations with any country.

Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Marianela Ferriol was asked at a weekly news briefing about reports Spain was to ask the 15-member EU to adopt its Cuba policy as a unified stance urging democractic reforms and respect for human rights.

Ferriol declined comment on the specific issue, saying "our rule is not to debate our bilateral relations in public and Spain is not going to be the exception." When Cuba felt the time was right, it would comment, she added.

But asked whether in general Cuba viewed as acceptable conditions placed on issues such as economic cooperation, Ferriol said Havana rejected this "totally and absolutely" and added: "We have never accepted any conditioning."
A Spanish Foreign Ministry official in Madrid said on Wednesday that Spain was to present its proposal to an EU committee meeting on Latin America in Brussels on Thursday.

Spain and Cuba have had close ties historically, but the new conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, which came to power in Madrid in May, has taken a tougher line than its Socialist predecessor.
Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said last week cooperation and aid to Cuba should be linked to political and economic liberalisation. He said Spain will urge the EU to link increases in aid to reforms.

The EU is already united in opposing the U.S. Helms-Burton law signed by President Bill Clinton in March, which gives U.S. citizens the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties formerly owned by Americans and nationalised after Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution.

Canada, a key investor and trading partner of Cuba, has also said its willingness to expand economic cooperation will depend on Cuba's willingness to respond to calls for political reforms and improvements on human rights.

Clinton is to decide early next year whether to suspend for a further period implementation of a section of the law that permits law suits against foreign companies. The Clinton administration has told allies Clinton would be willing to suspend that section further if the allies demonstrated they were taking some steps to push for reforms in Cuba.
